reference.source: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children, and Adolescents
clinicalPearls: Isolated cleft mitral valve is a slit in the anterior leaflet pointing towards the left ventricular outflow tract, distinct from the atrioventricular septal defect cleft, which points towards the ventricular septum.
It presents with mitral regurgitation ranging from an incidental finding to heart failure.
It is best seen on parasternal short-axis and 3D echocardiography as a V-shaped indentation in the leaflet during diastole.

Atrioventricular septal defect and other endocardial cushion anomalies must always be excluded, as the septal-type cleft accompanies a common atrioventricular junction with an inlet ventricular septal defect or ostium primum atrial septal defect.
The regurgitant jet often arises through the cleft and may be eccentric, so severity should be quantified carefully.
It is associated with conotruncal anomalies and heterotaxy in some patients.
Surgical closure with cleft suture, with or without annuloplasty, is the usual repair and is generally durable.
reference.pathophysiology: A cleft is a congenital slit-like division of a mitral leaflet, most often the anterior leaflet. An isolated cleft points towards the left ventricular outflow tract and is regarded as a distinct developmental anomaly of the mitral valve, whereas the cleft seen in atrioventricular septal defect represents the commissure between the left superior and inferior bridging leaflets of a common atrioventricular valve and points towards the ventricular septum. In both, the resulting failure of leaflet coaptation produces mitral regurgitation of variable severity, and chronic volume loading leads to left atrial and left ventricular dilatation.
additionalDifferentials: Partial or complete atrioventricular septal defect
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiography with parasternal short-axis imaging
Electrocardiography, where a left superior axis suggests the atrioventricular septal defect spectrum
Screening for ostium primum atrial septal defect and inlet ventricular septal defect
Cardiac catheterisation if pulmonary hypertension is suspected
redFlags: Severe mitral regurgitation with left ventricular dilatation or dysfunction
Heart failure symptoms or failure to thrive
Features of an associated atrioventricular septal defect with a significant shunt
reference.prognosis: An isolated cleft with mild regurgitation may remain stable, whereas significant regurgitation responds well to surgical cleft closure with good long-term durability, although some residual or recurrent regurgitation can occur.
pitfalls: Mislabelling an atrioventricular septal defect cleft as an isolated cleft despite its different orientation and associations
Missing the cleft on standard long-axis views when short-axis or 3D imaging is needed
Overlooking an associated ostium primum atrial septal defect
references: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children, and Adolescents
Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
management: Surgical cleft closure by direct suture repair is the definitive treatment for haemodynamically significant mitral regurgitation, with good long-term durability.
Medical heart-failure therapy with afterload reduction and diuretics to manage volume overload while awaiting or deferring surgery.
Serial echocardiography to quantify regurgitation severity and monitor left atrial and left ventricular dilatation, guiding the timing of intervention.
Systematic exclusion and management of associated atrioventricular septal defect, ostium primum atrial septal defect and inlet ventricular septal defect.
Surveillance for residual or recurrent regurgitation and for rhythm disturbance after repair.
Ongoing paediatric cardiology follow-up with attention to associated conotruncal and heterotaxy anomalies.
